## What This Tutorial Covers

`NaiveMFLFRMixDClust` fits Bayesian mixture models to mixed continuous/count/categorical
data via CAVI, automatically selecting the number of clusters and identifying which
features actually drive cluster structure. This tutorial walks through a complete
real-data application end to end:

1. Loading a real, public dataset (NHANES cardiometabolic risk factors).
2. Fitting the **Shared Feature Relevance Model (SFRM)**.
3. Fitting the **Local Feature Relevance Model (LFRM)**.
4. Reading the diagnostics - PIP and EIG - to decide which features matter and why.
5. Relating the result to an independently published analysis of similar data.

## The Dataset: NHANES Cardiometabolic Risk Factors {#sec-dataset}

The National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) is an ongoing public
health survey run by the U.S. CDC, combining interviews, physical examinations, and
laboratory tests. We use an extract of 11 cardiometabolic risk factors plus sex and
smoking status, for adults aged 40-59, from the **2017-2018 cycle**
[@cdc_nhanes_2017_2018]. This variable set mirrors @wang2026bayesian, an
independently published CAVI-based mixture model paper analyzing a similar extract.

The raw files are harmonized by `experiments/scripts/build_nhanes_dataset.py`;
the harmonized CSV is `experiments/data/nhanes_2017_2018_40_59.csv`.

## Setup

```{julia}
using NaiveMFLFRMixDClust
using CSV, DataFrames, Statistics, Random, Printf
```

## Loading and Preparing the Data

```{julia}
df = CSV.read(joinpath(@__DIR__, "../data/nhanes_2017_2018_40_59.csv"), DataFrame)
println("n = $(nrow(df)),  columns = $(names(df))")
first(df, 3)
```

```{julia}
feature_names = ["bmi", "height", "WHtR", "SBP", "DBP", "pulse",
                 "hdl", "non_HDL", "hba1c", "eGFR", "sex", "smoking"]

function onehot(val, levels)
    idx = findfirst(==(val), levels)
    isnothing(idx) && error("Value $val not in $levels")
    v = zeros(Int, length(levels)); v[idx] = 1; v
end

dataset = Vector{Any}(undef, 12)
cont_cols = [:bmi, :height, :WHtR, :SBP, :DBP, :pulse, :hdl, :non_HDL, :hba1c, :eGFR]
for (j, col) in enumerate(cont_cols)
    dataset[j] = Float64.(df[!, col])
end
dataset[11] = [onehot(x, ["male", "female"])             for x in df.sex]
dataset[12] = [onehot(x, ["never", "former", "current"]) for x in df.smoking]

for j in 1:10
    m = mean(dataset[j]); s = std(dataset[j])
    dataset[j] = (dataset[j] .- m) ./ s
end

println("n = $(nrow(df)), p = 12 (10 continuous + sex + smoking)")
println("Sex: $(count(==("male"), df.sex)) male, $(count(==("female"), df.sex)) female")
```

## Fitting the Model {#sec-fitting}

We fit both model settings with $K_{\text{fit}}=10$, $u^{(0)}=0.01$, letting the
sparse Dirichlet prior plus post-hoc pruning determine $\widehat{K}$ automatically.

### SFRM - Shared Feature Relevance Model

Under `SFRM()`, each feature has a single relevance probability shared across all clusters.

```{julia}
Random.seed!(42)
res_sfrm = mixClust(dataset, 10;
                    model_setting = SFRM(),
                    u0       = 0.01,
                    max_iter = 3000,
                    tol      = 1e-5,
                    compact  = true)

K_sfrm = size(res_sfrm.w, 2)
@printf("SFRM → K̂ = %d clusters (converged in %d / 3000 iterations)\n",
        K_sfrm, length(res_sfrm.elbo_history))
println("Cluster sizes: ", [count(==(k), res_sfrm.labels) for k in 1:K_sfrm])
```

### LFRM - Local Feature Relevance Model

Under `LFRM()`, relevance can differ cluster by cluster.

```{julia}
Random.seed!(42)
res_lfrm = mixClust(dataset, 10;
                    model_setting = LFRM(),
                    u0       = 0.01,
                    max_iter = 3000,
                    tol      = 1e-5,
                    compact  = true)

K_lfrm = size(res_lfrm.w, 2)
@printf("LFRM → K̂ = %d clusters (converged in %d / 3000 iterations)\n",
        K_lfrm, length(res_lfrm.elbo_history))
println("Cluster sizes: ", [count(==(k), res_lfrm.labels) for k in 1:K_lfrm])
```

### Feature Relevance - PIP

Two diagnostics, two different questions:

- **PIP** answers "is this feature active at all (modeled per cluster rather than pooled)?"
- **EIG** answers "how much does that inclusion actually separate the clusters?"

A feature can have high PIP yet low EIG - `sex` here is a clean example: the model
assigns it near-certain inclusion yet its EIG is modest, meaning it structures
individual cluster densities without strongly separating the cluster centroids.
Note also that `smoking` is essentially *excluded* by SFRM (PIP ≈ 0): the relevance
mechanism finds no cluster-level signal worth modeling separately, without any manual
intervention.

```{julia}
plot_pips(res_sfrm; feature_names = feature_names,
          title = "Posterior Inclusion Probabilities - SFRM")
```

```{julia}
plot_pips(res_lfrm; feature_names = feature_names,
          title = "Posterior Inclusion Probabilities - LFRM")
```

### Feature Relevance - EIG

```{julia}
eig_sfrm = compute_eig(res_sfrm.margins, res_sfrm.w, res_sfrm.pip)
plot_eig(eig_sfrm, 0.20; feature_names = feature_names,
         title = "Expected Information Gain - SFRM  (τ = 0.20)")
```

```{julia}
eig_lfrm = compute_eig(res_lfrm.margins, res_lfrm.w, res_lfrm.pip)
plot_eig(eig_lfrm, 0.20; feature_names = feature_names,
         title = "Expected Information Gain - LFRM  (τ = 0.20)")
```

```{julia}
active_sfrm = filter_features(eig_sfrm, 0.20)
active_lfrm = filter_features(eig_lfrm, 0.20)
println("SFRM active (EIG ≥ 0.20): ", feature_names[active_sfrm])
println("LFRM active (EIG ≥ 0.20): ", feature_names[active_lfrm])
```

### Local PIPs (LFRM) {#sec-local-pips}

```{julia}
plot_local_pips(res_lfrm; feature_names = feature_names,
                title = "Per-Cluster Mean PIPs - LFRM")
```

### Subtype Feature Profiles

```{julia}
plot_profiles(res_sfrm, dataset; feature_names = feature_names,
              title = "Feature Profiles - SFRM")
```

```{julia}
plot_profiles(res_lfrm, dataset; feature_names = feature_names,

```

Reading across rows recovers recognizable phenotypes: a low-eGFR cluster (impaired
kidney function), a high-HbA1c cluster (hyperglycemia), BMI/WHtR-elevated clusters
of differing severity - broadly consistent with @wang2026bayesian and
@lhoste2024cardiometabolic.

### Cluster Assignments in Feature Space

BMI (feature 1) vs HbA1c (feature 9) - the two strongest discriminators.

```{julia}
plot_assignments(res_sfrm, dataset;
                 x_feature = 1, y_feature = 9,
                 feature_names = feature_names,
                 title = "Cluster Assignments - SFRM (BMI vs HbA1c)")
```

```{julia}
plot_assignments(res_lfrm, dataset;
                 x_feature = 1, y_feature = 9,
                 feature_names = feature_names,
                 title = "Cluster Assignments - LFRM (BMI vs HbA1c)")
```

## Sex as a Feature, Not a Filter {#sec-sex-as-feature}

It is standard practice to exclude sex by restricting the sample
(@wang2026bayesian study males 40-59 only), because sex differences in body
composition and cholesterol can dominate cluster formation. With `NaiveMFLFRMixDClust` you
have another option: include `sex` as a Multinomial feature and let the relevance
mechanism tell you directly whether it dominates.

```{julia}
idx_sex = findfirst(==("sex"), feature_names)
@printf("sex - SFRM: PIP = %.3f,  EIG = %.3f\n",
        mean(res_sfrm.pip[:, idx_sex]), eig_sfrm[idx_sex])
@printf("sex - LFRM: PIP = %.3f,  EIG = %.3f\n",
        mean(res_lfrm.pip[:, idx_sex]), eig_lfrm[idx_sex])
```

Under SFRM, `sex` has a high PIP - the model detects that sex should be modeled
per cluster rather than pooled - but its EIG is low, indicating that despite being
selected as relevant, it contributes modest discriminatory power between clusters
overall. Under LFRM the picture is similar: EIG remains small. **This is itself an
informative result.** Including `sex` does not distort the clustering: the dominant
drivers (BMI, WHtR, HbA1c) emerge regardless, and the relevance mechanism reports,
quantitatively, that the sex effect on cluster separation is limited. A relevance-aware
model can accommodate a potentially confounding variable and answer the question
directly - without requiring prior exclusion by design.

## Relating This to Published Work {#sec-nhanes-comparison}

@wang2026bayesian fit a CAVI-based mixture model to a similar NHANES extract
(pooled 1988-2018, males 40-59 only). Their likelihood treats every feature as fully
informative in every cluster - no background/active switch, no relevance mechanism.
They fix $K=10$ a priori (from a separate K-means analysis), even though their
posterior mixture weights show two components with negligible mass ($\pi \approx
0.001$), and no quantitative diagnostic equivalent to PIP or EIG is available.

Despite these differences, both analyses recover broadly the same phenotype
categories - hyperglycemia-dominant, obesity/elevated-BMI, near-median "typical,"
lipid- or renal-marker-distinguished clusters. The comparison illustrates what an
explicit relevance mechanism buys in practice: automatic order selection, a direct
quantitative answer to "does this variable matter," and the ability to detect
redistributable cluster-specific effects.

## Takeaways

- Fit **both** SFRM and LFRM as a matter of course; the comparison of which
  features change EIG - and by how much - is informative in itself.
- Read **PIP** as "should this feature be modeled per cluster at all" and **EIG**
  as "how much does that inclusion actually separate clusters" - they answer
  different questions and can disagree (`sex` above has high PIP but low EIG; `smoking`
  is excluded entirely by SFRM despite being a plausible risk-factor a priori).
- A relevance mechanism gives a real alternative to manually excluding a suspected
  confound: model it explicitly and let the diagnostics tell you whether the concern
  was warranted, and whether it is global (SFRM) or local to specific clusters (LFRM).
- The sparse-Dirichlet-prior-plus-pruning pipeline removes the need for a separate
  K-means step just to pick $K$ before fitting the model.
